topic: AI-assisted software development; longitudinal quality and maintenance outcomes
status: bounded cross-paper synthesis; broad absence claim rejected; global novelty unverified
claim: It is no longer accurate to say long-term AI/software outcomes are unstudied: by 2026 there are studies of two-year IDE telemetry, SATD lifecycle across LLM/ML/non-ML repositories, and static-analysis issues in explicitly AI-attributed GitHub commits. The more limited open problem supported by this sample is triangulating causal AI exposure with semantic code quality and maintenance outcomes under a credible human-only or within-project comparison. These studies measure different constructs and do not jointly resolve that question.
positive_evidence: The sampled 2026 SLR searches 2020–2024 only and includes 87 primary studies, so it cannot establish the absence of 2026 longitudinal work.
A 2026 IDE-log study tracks 800 devices over Oct 2022–Oct 2024 and supplements logs with a 62-person survey and five interviews.
A 2026 SATD study compares 159 LLM, 159 ML, and 159 traditional Python repositories and analyzes millions of comment events with survival analysis.
A 2026 wild-code study reports 304,362 explicitly AI-attributed commits across 6,275 public GitHub repositories and follows static-analysis issues over time.
counterevidence: The IDE-log authors explicitly say their goal is not causal attribution; productivity is proxied by typed characters and code quality by debugging events, not eventual correctness of committed code.
The SATD study measures admitted comments rather than all technical debt; 44% of sampled comments were false-positive, undefined, or unknown, and repository age confounds LLM-versus-ML comparisons.

The wild-code study has no clean human-authored baseline, relies on explicit Git attribution, covers popular public projects in Python/JavaScript/TypeScript, and measures only static-analysis-detectable code issues.
The earlier SLR still identifies an evidence shortage through its 2024 cutoff, so the correction is temporal, not a claim that research is complete.

falsifiable_test: Pre-register a prospective multi-project study that records AI-assistance exposure at the task/commit level, compares within-developer or matched within-repository AI-assisted and non-assisted changes, and follows changes for at least 12 months. Blind reviewers should adjudicate defects and security findings; use project tests plus independent behavioral tests; measure repair time, issue survival, review intensity, severity, and change size. Adjust for task, developer, repository maturity, language, tool/model, and adoption timing. The gap claim weakens if existing open datasets already provide these linked exposure, semantic-outcome, and counterfactual measures with robust sensitivity analyses, or if matched estimates show no material difference.
limitations: This is a literature synthesis from a purposive sample and a targeted 2026 follow-up, not a systematic review or causal result. Constructs and populations differ substantially; the proposed design lead is not a verified novelty claim.

topic: automated repair; benchmark realism and distribution shift
status: bounded empirical design lead; not a global novelty claim
claim: In the sampled Excel formula repair study, the 618-example synthetic benchmark is substantially easier than its 59-example real seed across four tested models, despite broader function/error diversity. Together with transformed-Defects4J generalization loss in the random sample, this supports testing repair systems on difficulty-stratified, held-out real tasks rather than using synthetic scale or lexical diversity as a proxy for external validity.
positive_evidence: FoRepBench versus seed execution-match: GPT-4.1 0.80 vs 0.41; GPT-4o 0.73 vs 0.35; Phi-3 0.58 vs 0.24; Mistral 0.51 vs 0.19.
The Excel paper attributes the difference to shallower nesting and fewer semantic transformations in generated examples; it also finds human/LLM validation disagreement.
The sampled transformed-Defects4J paper finds mean correct/plausible fix declines of 49.48%/42.90% across 11 open models; 10/12 model-prompt configurations remain below original-set results.
counterevidence: FoRepBench increases error/function diversity and is a useful low-cost data-augmentation resource; lower seed performance does not invalidate its value for in-distribution training.
The real seed has only 59 examples, so its performance estimate is noisy and may reflect selection effects.
Defects4J transformations and Excel forum seeds represent different tasks; the results cannot be pooled or generalized to all repair benchmarks.

Benchmark-validity research is established: PatchDiff reports plausible SWE-bench patches that diverge behaviorally from references and some counted-correct patches that fail developer tests. This is not an undiscovered general problem.

sources.title: Are ‘Solved Issues’ in SWE-bench Really Solved Correctly? An Empirical Study

falsifiable_test: Construct multi-domain repair evaluation sets with task difficulty independently rated before model runs. Hold out repositories and time periods; compare synthetic-only, real-only, and mixed training at equal data/model budgets. Report pass@k, hidden tests, differential behavior against both reference patches and independent specifications, severity-weighted defects, and rank stability by difficulty stratum. The lead weakens if synthetic-trained systems transfer to held-out real tasks without a material difficulty-conditioned performance gap across domains and oracles.
limitations: This finding joins two non-equivalent repair tasks and a literature counterexample; it motivates a design test but does not estimate a universal synthetic-to-real gap or establish the absence of prior work.

status: known evaluation limitation; bounded application lead, not a novelty claim
claim: The sampled SATD-repair study improves granularity by scoring changed lines against a later developer patch, but does not functionally test generated repairs; the sampled Excel study shows executable/contextual validation disagreement, while PatchDiff independently shows reference behavior and benchmark tests can disagree. A practical SATD-repair evaluation should combine patch-overlap diagnostics with executable, specification-grounded behavioral checks and blind semantic review.
positive_evidence: SATD paper reports whole-code overlap metrics may reward leaving buggy input unchanged; its LEMOD metric compares line-level edits with one later developer patch, but generated repairs are not evaluated with functional tests.

The Excel paper's validator agrees with each human annotator at κ=0.42 in its results table and accepts some execution-consistent but contextually implausible examples; its conclusion reports a conflicting κ=0.25.

PatchDiff study reports 7.8% of tested SWE-bench plausible patches counted correct while failing developer tests; 29.6% differ behaviorally from ground-truth patches, and manual reviewers deem 28.6% of divergent patches certainly incorrect.
counterevidence: Reference patches and edit-level overlap remain useful for reproducible partial-credit comparisons; they are not worthless merely because they do not prove semantics.
PatchDiff is a specific SWE-bench/three-tool study and its divergent behaviors are not all necessarily incorrect.
The proposed multi-oracle evaluation is a design implication; comparable SATD studies may already exist outside the targeted follow-up search.

Are ‘Solved Issues’ in SWE-bench Really Solved Correctly? An Empirical Study

falsifiable_test: For an independently reviewed sample of SATD tasks, evaluate generated changes with (1) line-level reference overlap, (2) original and hidden regression tests, (3) differential execution against a written behavioral specification, and (4) blinded expert judgments of intent/maintainability. Estimate agreement and model ranking under each endpoint, stratify by patch size/task difficulty, and release disagreements. The practical lead weakens if overlap scores reliably predict hidden-test/specification correctness and expert ratings across repositories and models.
limitations: Evidence is distributed across unlike repair domains, and no new SATD semantic-validation experiment was run here. This is not a claim that reference-based metrics are invalid or that the proposed triangulation is globally novel.
